cards.question: Who introduced 'energy' into physics in its modern sense, and when?
cards.answer: The Scottish physicist William Rankine, in 1852.

cards.question: What does 'energy' denote?
cards.answer: The ability of a system to produce an (external) effect.

cards.question: Name the four kinds of energy the lecture distinguishes.
cards.answer: Mechanical, thermal, electrical and chemical energy.

cards.question: What is a kilowatt-hour in joules, and why is it used?
cards.answer: 1 kWh is 3.6 million joules; it is the billing unit for electricity, gas, etc.

cards.question: What is 1 kg SKE (coal equivalent)?
cards.answer: The energy released by burning 1 kg of hard coal (8.141 kWh, 29 MJ); a common unit for stating primary energy quantities.

cards.question: Roughly how much electricity does a European household need per year?
cards.answer: About 3,500 to 5,000 kWh per year.

cards.question: List the four stages of the energy chain from source to use.
cards.answer: Primary energy, secondary energy, final energy, useful energy.

cards.question: What is primary energy?
cards.answer: The energy resource in its natural form, e.g. crude oil.

cards.question: What is secondary energy?
cards.answer: Transformed primary energy.

cards.question: What is final energy?
cards.answer: The energy delivered to the end user.

cards.question: What is useful energy?
cards.answer: The energy that actually serves the need at the end of the chain, e.g. heat, light or motion, after the last conversion.

cards.question: What is the difference between the higher and the lower heating value?
cards.answer: Higher (gross) heating value: the water in the exhaust is liquid, so condensation heat is included. Lower (net) heating value: the water stays gaseous.

cards.question: Why must you be careful with units when comparing fuels?
cards.answer: Fuels are quoted per kg or per m³ and with higher or lower heating value, so values are not directly comparable.

cards.question: Which fossil fuel has the lowest CO₂ emissions per kWh: hard coal, lignite, natural gas, oil or wood?
cards.answer: Natural gas, at about 0.2 kg CO₂ per kWh.

cards.question: Why can wood have CO₂ emissions of zero in the fuel table?
cards.answer: Because its carbon was taken from the air while the tree grew, so it can be counted as climate-neutral.

cards.question: State the first law of thermodynamics.
cards.answer: The total energy of an isolated system is constant; energy can be converted between forms but neither created nor destroyed.

cards.question: Describe the first law for a system without matter transfer: what changes the internal energy?
cards.answer: The change in internal energy equals heat gained from outside minus the work the system does on its surroundings.

cards.question: State the second law of thermodynamics.
cards.answer: The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases and stays constant only if all processes are reversible; changes proceed towards equilibrium, the state of maximum entropy.

cards.question: What is entropy?
cards.answer: A measure of the thermal energy per unit temperature that is not available for doing useful work.

cards.question: Summarise the first and second law in one sentence each.
cards.answer: First law: the total amount of energy is conserved. Second law: the overall quality of energy decreases over time (entropy).

cards.question: Give an example of an irreversible process.
cards.answer: When a hot and a cold body touch, heat flows from hot to cold until equilibrium; it never reverses spontaneously.

cards.question: What is a reversible process, and does it exist in reality?
cards.answer: A process that can go to another state and back to the initial state with no change to system or surroundings; it is idealised and never truly achieved.

cards.question: What does the Carnot efficiency limit say, and what does it depend on?
cards.answer: The maximum efficiency of a heat engine is always below Carnot efficiency, which depends only on the hot and cold temperatures (one minus cold over hot, in kelvin).

cards.question: In the heating-chain exercise, why is a heat pump on CCGT electricity better than burning gas directly, and an electric heating element on CCGT electricity worse?
cards.answer: A heat pump multiplies the electricity by its COP of 3, using less gas than direct burning; resistance heating at 60 % CCGT efficiency needs more gas than direct burning.

cards.question: In the renewable-electricity chain exercise, which route needs the least electricity and which are to be avoided?
cards.answer: Direct electric heating (or heat pump) needs least; routes via methane or hydrogen and back to electricity waste the most and should not be pursued for heat.

cards.question: What is the substitution method for primary energy demand?
cards.answer: Renewable and nuclear electricity is counted as the fossil fuel that would have been needed to produce it at typical plant efficiency.

cards.question: Why can the situation be viewed more optimistically than primary energy demand suggests?
cards.answer: Primary energy counts large conversion losses of fossil fuels; renewable electricity and electrification are far more efficient, so final and primary demand fall.

cards.question: Rank battery electric, fuel cell hydrogen and PtL combustion cars by how much renewable electricity reaches the wheels.
cards.answer: Battery electric vehicles are best (about 69 %), then hydrogen fuel cell (about 26 %), then combustion on power-to-liquid fuel (about 13 %).

cards.question: Why is the battery electric car so much more efficient than the hydrogen or PtL car?
cards.answer: It avoids the conversion losses of electrolysis, hydrogen compression and transport, and fuel cell or combustion engine.

cards.question: What are new drivers of energy demand growth mentioned in the lecture?
cards.answer: Data centers are major new drivers of electricity demand.

cards.question: Give the key findings about the global energy system.
cards.answer: Fossil fuels still dominate; electricity has made good progress with renewables and nuclear; decarbonisation is huge; electrification gives big efficiency gains; data centers raise demand.

cards.question: What is OPEC?
cards.answer: The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries: a cartel of 14 oil-producing countries founded in Baghdad in 1960.

cards.question: What is the IEA, when was it founded and why?
cards.answer: The International Energy Agency, representing 28 industrialised countries, founded in 1973 in response to the first oil crisis; main publication: World Energy Outlook.

cards.question: What are the Energy Watch Group and dena?
cards.answer: EWG: an international network of independent scientists and parliamentarians studying resource depletion and renewable scenarios. dena: the German Energy Agency, a majority state-owned competence center for efficiency and renewables.

cards.question: What are the UBA and the AGEB?
cards.answer: UBA: the German Environment Agency, Europe's largest environmental authority. AGEB: the Working Group on Energy Balances, which publishes Germany's annual energy balance.

cards.question: In Germany's public net electricity generation in 2025, which source was number one and what share was renewable?
cards.answer: Onshore wind was number one, and renewables were about 55.9 % of public net generation.

cards.question: What happened to photovoltaics in Germany's 2025 electricity ranking?
cards.answer: PV moved into second place for the first time, ahead of lignite.

cards.question: What milestone did renewables reach in global electricity generation in 2025?
cards.answer: Renewables (33.8 %) exceeded coal (33.0 %) for the first time in over 100 years.

cards.question: What does 'clean power has decoupled demand from fossils' mean?
cards.answer: Demand growth is now met by clean sources while fossil generation stalls, unlike the early 2000s when fossil growth met demand growth.

cards.question: What are full-load hours and the capacity factor?
cards.answer: Full-load hours are the hours per year a plant would need at full power to produce its annual energy; capacity factor is that divided by the 8760 hours in a year.

cards.question: A plant runs the whole year at half power. How does that compare with running half the year at full power?
cards.answer: The two are equivalent: both give 4380 full-load hours and a capacity factor of 0.5.

cards.question: What are the key levers for decarbonising heat, transport and industry?
cards.answer: Expansion of renewable energies, electrification, efficiency, and synthetic fuels where reasonable.

cards.question: What happens to electricity demand by 2045 in the German scenario although final energy falls in every sector?
cards.answer: Net electricity consumption roughly doubles (507 to 993 TWh), because electrification and hydrogen/PtX move demand to electricity.

cards.question: Why could final energy demand in transport and buildings fall so sharply?
cards.answer: Efficiency chains: electric motors and heat pumps are much more efficient than combustion engines and boilers.

cards.question: Name the four global decarbonisation steps in order.
cards.answer: Improve efficiency everywhere; 100 % renewable electricity; electrify transport and heating as far as possible; Power-to-X for what cannot be electrified.

cards.question: Define energy efficiency.
cards.answer: Providing the same level of service with less energy input, or better service for the same energy.

cards.question: Contrast the goals of the thermal insulation ordinances and the heating systems ordinances.
cards.answer: Insulation ordinances reduce useful energy demand through structural building measures; heating systems ordinances reduce final energy through technical improvements such as boiler efficiency.

cards.question: Name examples of structural measures to reduce a building's useful energy demand.
cards.answer: Improved insulation, avoiding leaks, and double-glazed windows.

cards.question: How did the 2026 Buildings Energy Act change (GModG) differ from the earlier 65 % rule?
cards.answer: The old rule regulated the appliance (at least 65 % renewable heating); the new law allows gas or oil boilers again but regulates the fuel, which must become climate-neutral step by step until 100 % by 2045.

cards.question: How much has the allowed primary energy demand of new German residential buildings fallen since 1977?
cards.answer: By roughly a factor of six, from about 270 to about 45 kWh per square metre per year.

cards.question: Name the demonstration building standards that were ahead of the law.
cards.answer: Low-energy house, 3-litre house, passive house, zero-energy and plus-energy house.

cards.question: Why did German industrial emissions fall towards the 2030 target according to UBA, and is that real progress?
cards.answer: Mainly because of production declines and lower energy use, not decarbonisation; the fuel mix barely changed.

cards.question: Which two industries are named as hard to decarbonise, with their global CO₂ share?
cards.answer: Iron and steel (over 7 % of emissions) and cement (about 3 % of global emissions).

cards.question: Why is carbon in the blast furnace route a reagent rather than just a fuel?
cards.answer: Carbon removes the oxygen from iron ore, producing CO₂ as a product of the reaction, so running on wind power would not remove the CO₂.

cards.question: What is 'green steel' and what comes out instead of CO₂?
cards.answer: Steel made by direct reduction of iron ore with hydrogen; the by-product is water vapour (steam) instead of carbon dioxide.

cards.question: Give an example of a green-steel project mentioned in the lecture.
cards.answer: The Swedish HYBRIT project (SSAB), reducing iron with hydrogen.

cards.question: Where does the CO₂ in cement production come from, and which part can renewable electricity fix?
cards.answer: About one third from the fuel (fixable with renewable electricity), about two thirds from the rock (limestone calcination, CaCO₃ to CaO and CO₂), which is process-related.

cards.question: What option remains for unavoidable cement CO₂ emissions?
cards.answer: Carbon capture and storage (CCS).

cards.question: Comparing a 250 km trip, which has the lowest CO₂: diesel car, electric car on the German grid mix, or the train?
cards.answer: The train, with an electric car on the grid mix in between, and the diesel car the highest; occupancy also matters.

cards.question: Why do we need Power-to-X?
cards.answer: For applications where electrification is not possible, such as aviation, shipping and some industrial processes.

cards.question: What is the misconception in listing fossil and renewable energy sources only?
cards.answer: Storage was missing: fossil fuels are stored solar energy of the past; renewables need storage to provide energy on demand.

cards.question: What is the 'residue cycle of energy and materials'?
cards.answer: Recycling in the energy sector: moving from one-way fossil use to synthetic fuels and Power-to-X so residues and CO₂ are recycled.

cards.question: What is the 'colour theory' of hydrogen about?
cards.answer: Classifying hydrogen by its production route, e.g. green from renewable electricity versus grey from fossil gas.

cards.question: What is Power-to-X and what does it need besides renewable electricity?
cards.answer: Converting renewable electricity into hydrogen and further products such as fuels and chemicals; the carbon-based ones need renewable carbon, e.g. CO₂ from air or biomass.

cards.question: Why are full-load hours decisive for the cost of renewable PtX?
cards.answer: High full-load hours mean the expensive electrolysers run more, so sites with hybrid PV and wind (and hydro or geothermal) are best.

cards.question: Where should hydrogen be used most effectively?
cards.answer: Where direct electrification is hard, such as industry feedstock, steel, shipping and aviation, not in passenger cars.

cards.question: Name the four fossil conversion machines in Chapter 4 and their output.
cards.answer: Steam turbine (electricity and heat), gas turbine (electricity and heat), boiler (heat only) and refinery (fuel).

cards.question: Which two machines convert heat into electricity and what limits their efficiency?
cards.answer: The steam turbine and the gas turbine; the temperature (Carnot limit).

cards.question: Why does raising the steam temperature or lowering the cooling temperature raise the Carnot limit?
cards.answer: The Carnot efficiency is one minus cold over hot temperature in kelvin, so hotter heat source or colder sink gives a higher limit.

cards.question: Why must temperatures be in kelvin in the Carnot formula?
cards.answer: Because the formula needs absolute temperature; 0 K is -273.15 °C, and a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.

cards.question: Order geothermal, nuclear, hard coal and combustion turbine by Carnot efficiency.
cards.answer: Geothermal lowest (about 37 %), nuclear (50 %), hard coal (62 %), combustion turbine highest (78 %).

cards.question: Which cycle describes a steam turbine and how does it work in one line?
cards.answer: The Clausius-Rankine cycle: burn fuel outside the loop, boil water, spin the turbine.

cards.question: List the four steps of the Clausius-Rankine cycle.
cards.answer: Pump the liquid to high pressure; heat it in the boiler to vapour; expand it through the turbine; condense it in the condenser and release heat to the heat sink.

cards.question: Why does the pump in the Rankine cycle need little energy?
cards.answer: Because the working fluid is a liquid at that stage.

cards.question: Why should steam remain vapour in the turbine?
cards.answer: To avoid damage to the turbine (pitting) from droplets, which limits how much enthalpy can be extracted.

cards.question: What are the Carnot and real efficiency of a hard coal steam plant?
cards.answer: Carnot about 62.5 %, real about 33 to 45 %.

cards.question: Which cycle describes a gas turbine and how does it work in one line?
cards.answer: The Brayton cycle: burn the fuel inside the machine and let the hot gas spin the turbine directly.

cards.question: List the steps of the Brayton cycle.
cards.answer: Compressor compresses the air; fuel is burned at constant pressure in the combustion chamber; hot gas expands in the turbine; hot exhaust leaves to the heat sink.

cards.question: Why is air compressed before combustion in a gas turbine?
cards.answer: Compressing the fuel-air mixture greatly improves the thermodynamic efficiency.

cards.question: What are the material limits of gas turbines and how are they handled?
cards.answer: Inlet temperatures up to about 1,500 °C exceed the melting point of nickel superalloys (around 1,300 °C); air film cooling and thermal barrier coatings such as yttrium or zirconium oxide are used.

cards.question: Why does a gas turbine only reach about 40 % although its Carnot limit is about 80 %?
cards.answer: Material limits keep the temperature low, and the hot exhaust (450 to 650 °C) is thrown away as waste heat.

cards.question: What is a combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) plant?
cards.answer: A gas turbine (Brayton) whose hot exhaust drives a steam (Rankine) bottoming cycle through a heat recovery steam generator.

cards.question: What real efficiency does a CCGT reach compared with a single gas turbine?
cards.answer: About 50 to 63 % for a CCGT versus about 35 to 42 % for a gas turbine alone.

cards.question: Which turbines can run on hydrogen, and how?
cards.answer: Gas turbines can burn hydrogen in the combustor (with modifications), steam turbines can use hydrogen-fired boilers; also CCGTs.

cards.question: What does a boiler produce and why is it efficient?
cards.answer: Heat only; it has no turbine, so there are no heat-to-electricity losses.

cards.question: Name the main components of a central heating system with a boiler.
cards.answer: The boiler, a distribution system (pipes, pumps, valves) and a heat sink such as radiators.

cards.question: What does a refinery do?
cards.answer: It does not burn crude oil but re-shapes it into fuels and other products.

cards.question: How does a nuclear plant differ from a coal steam plant?
cards.answer: Same steam turbine process, only the heat source changes: fission in a reactor instead of a fire.

cards.question: What is the engineering problem in a nuclear chain reaction?
cards.answer: Control, not release: holding the chain reaction at exactly one (critical).

cards.question: Compare boiling water and pressurised water reactors.
cards.answer: BWR: water boils inside the reactor in one loop and steam goes directly to the turbine. PWR: water stays liquid under high pressure and a second, separate loop makes the steam.

cards.question: Why can nuclear plants not simply run hotter?
cards.answer: Fuel cladding limits the steam temperature to about 300 °C, so nuclear trades efficiency for safety margin.

cards.question: What is the economics of nuclear power versus gas?
cards.answer: Nuclear is the mirror image of gas: high capital cost paid before any kWh and very low fuel cost; gas has low capital cost and high fuel cost.

cards.question: Name the primary energies and conversion technologies in the overview of renewable conversion.
cards.answer: Sun (PV, solar thermal power, solar heat), wind (wind turbine), water (hydropower, ocean), biomass (power plant, biofuel, pellet heating), geothermal (power or heat plant).

cards.question: What does 'global radiation' mean?
cards.answer: Total radiation on a horizontal surface: direct plus diffuse, not 'worldwide'.

cards.question: Roughly how much does a desert site receive compared to Germany?
cards.answer: About twice as much (about 2,300 versus 1,100 kWh/m² per year).

cards.question: Why does PV work in Bavaria but concentrated solar needs a desert?
cards.answer: Panels use diffuse light; mirrors can only concentrate direct radiation.

cards.question: Why silicon, with a band gap of 1.12 eV?
cards.answer: It is in the middle of the solar spectrum: loose enough for sunlight to free electrons, tight enough that each electron carries useful voltage.

cards.question: Explain how a solar cell makes electricity in one line.
cards.answer: Light creates charge carriers via the photoelectric effect and the junction turns them into a current.

cards.question: What is the Shockley-Queisser limit?
cards.answer: The maximum efficiency of a single-junction solar cell, about 33 %, set by the band gap compromise.

cards.question: Give the three numbers: theoretical limit, best cell ever, module typical.
cards.answer: 33 % physics limit, 27 % best cell ever made, about 20.7 % for a commercial module.

cards.question: Why does a band gap set too low or too high lose energy?
cards.answer: Too low: nearly all photons absorbed but most of each is wasted as heat. Too high: each photon pays well but most pass straight through.

cards.question: Why are solar cells connected in series, and what is the catch?
cards.answer: Voltage adds up (72 cells give about 41 V) which an inverter can use; but all cells carry the same current, so the weakest or shaded cell limits the string.

cards.question: What are the commercial solar cell types and their module efficiencies?
cards.answer: Monocrystalline 20-22 %, polycrystalline 15-20 %, thin-film 5-15 %, tandem over 30 % (lab 44 %), organic about 10 %.

cards.question: What are the advantages of thin-film modules?
cards.answer: Simple production (vapour deposition), can be applied to glass or flexible lightweight materials, but lower efficiency.

cards.question: List the components of a PV system from modules to grid.
cards.answer: PV modules, MPP tracker, inverter, bidirectional meter, grid and household loads; optional charge controller and battery.

cards.question: Where does direct current end in a PV system?
cards.answer: At the inverter, which is the boundary between DC and AC.

cards.question: What can you do with surplus PV electricity?
cards.answer: Feed it into the grid at the EEG tariff, sell it via direct marketing, charge a battery, use it thermally, or curtail.

cards.question: Why do batteries sell with home PV?
cards.answer: Direct use is worth the retail price while exported electricity earns the much lower feed-in tariff; a battery moves midday surplus to the evening.

cards.question: Does a battery generate extra electricity?
cards.answer: No, it only shifts the same electricity in time.

cards.question: What are PV tracking systems?
cards.answer: Systems that follow the sun with one axis or two axes to increase yield.

cards.question: What are standard test conditions (STC) for PV modules?
cards.answer: Cell temperature 25 °C, irradiance 1,000 W/m², and spectrum AM 1.5.

cards.question: What does kWp mean?
cards.answer: Kilowatt peak: the rated power under standard test conditions.

cards.question: Describe the I-V curve of a solar module and its four key numbers.
cards.answer: Isc (short-circuit current, no voltage) and Voc (open-circuit voltage, no current) are the ends; Vmp and Imp give the maximum power point Pmax, the biggest rectangle under the curve.

cards.question: What does an MPP tracker do?
cards.answer: It adjusts current and voltage so the module always delivers maximum power for the current irradiance.

cards.question: How does temperature affect PV output?
cards.answer: Power falls with higher cell temperature (about -0.34 % per °C); a cold clear spring day beats a hot summer day, and deserts are not the easy answer.

cards.question: What is NMOT and why is it printed on the datasheet?
cards.answer: Nominal module operating temperature conditions (800 W/m², 20 °C air, 1 m/s wind): a realistic day, giving about 25 % less power than at STC.

cards.question: What affects the PV orientation yield, and what do south, flat and east/west roofs give?
cards.answer: South at about 37° tilt is optimal; flat and east or west lose some yield but are not far off; even north gives yield thanks to diffuse radiation.

cards.question: What four groups of influences determine PV feed-in power?
cards.answer: Earth geometry and rotation, surrounding terrain, atmospheric attenuation, and ambient temperature.

cards.question: Describe the variability of PV generation.
cards.answer: Fluctuations up to 80 % in under a minute, summer about four times winter, and strong day-to-day fluctuations.

cards.question: Why do full-load hours of PV differ by location?
cards.answer: Southern Germany about 900-1130 kWh/kWp, desert regions over 2,000, because of irradiation.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Contrast low-temperature solar heat with high-temperature solar thermal power.
cards.answer: Low temperature (60-90 °C) uses collectors for direct heat with no Carnot limit; high temperature (400-600 °C) uses concentrating mirrors for steam and a turbine, which is Carnot-limited.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: What does concentration of sunlight achieve?
cards.answer: It does not collect more light, it raises the temperature, which a heat engine needs.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Compare solar thermal and PV on the same roof.
cards.answer: Solar thermal gives heat at 40-60 % efficiency with cheap storage but local use only; PV gives electricity at about 21 % with expensive storage but grid transport.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: What is concentrated solar power (CSP)?
cards.answer: Concentrating sunlight to boil water and drive a steam turbine, like a coal plant with mirrors.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: What is the advantage of a parabolic trough plant with storage?
cards.answer: It stores heat rather than electricity, so it can generate after sunset.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Why did CSP growth stop?
cards.answer: PV fell in price faster than CSP; CSP is more complex and needs direct radiation, about half of which in Germany is diffuse.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: State the power law of wind energy.
cards.answer: Power is proportional to air density, rotor area and the cube of wind speed.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: How does wind speed change with height, and what is surface roughness?
cards.answer: It increases logarithmically with height; rough surfaces such as forest or city brake the wind, so taller towers pay off.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: What is the Betz limit?
cards.answer: 59.3 % (16/27): the maximum share of wind kinetic energy any turbine can extract; real turbines get about 45-50 %.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Why does the Betz limit exist?
cards.answer: Extracting all kinetic energy would leave the air at rest behind the rotor, so no further air could pass through; the optimum slows the wind to one third.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Describe the power characteristic of a wind turbine.
cards.answer: No output below cut-in speed, rising with wind speed to rated power, constant to cut-out speed (storm shutdown).

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Why is wind better near the coast?
cards.answer: Unobstructed wind over smooth water and local compensation flows from land-sea temperature differences.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Order PV rooftop, PV ground, onshore wind, offshore wind and biomass by full-load hours.
cards.answer: PV rooftop lowest, then PV ground, onshore wind, offshore wind, biomass highest.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: How does a solid biomass power plant work and why does it count as renewable?
cards.answer: Wood chips are burned, boiler steam drives a Rankine turbine (33 % electricity, 52 % heat); the carbon was taken from the air by the growing trees.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: How does a biogas plant work?
cards.answer: Bacteria digest wet biomass in a digester without air to make biogas (55 % methane); a gas engine CHP burns it for 40 % electricity and 44 % heat.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Why can biogas cut emissions that would have happened anyway?
cards.answer: It captures methane from slurry and burns it to CO₂; methane warms the planet about 80 times more than CO₂ over 20 years.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Eight of twelve generation technologies share one principle. What is it?
cards.answer: Make something hot, boil water, spin a turbine; only PV skips the heat engine.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: What limits wind, PV and coal efficiency respectively?
cards.answer: Wind: Betz limit; PV: Shockley-Queisser limit; coal: Carnot with the steam temperature capped by materials near 600 °C.

cards.topic: Ch5 Renewable Energies (Solar thermal, CSP, Wind, Biomass)
cards.question: Which generation technology has the highest efficiency, and which has the highest full-load hours?
cards.answer: Hydropower (85-90 %); geothermal has the highest full-load hours, about 7,500.
